title: Infra GPU Fleet, Capacity, IaC and CI/CD Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview:
This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference's recommended practices for GPU fleet sizing and capacity planning, cloud account and networking layout, Terraform / IaC modules, CI/CD and build pipelines, and operational runbooks. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for maintained prediction capacity across Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployment modes.

Goals:
- Keep production p95 generation latency within SLOs while minimizing unit cost per token.
- Provide reproducible, auditable IaC and CI/CD for fleet changes.
- Reduce incident MTTR with clear runbooks and ownership.

Contents:
1) Fleet capacity Planning and Targets
2) Cloud accounts, VPCs and Networking guidelines
3) Terraform / IaC module conventions and example usage
4) CI/CD and build pipeline patterns for infra changes
5) Runbooks for common GPU-fleet incidents
6) Ownership, metrics and operational telemetry

1) Fleet capacity planning and targets
Intro: Capacity planning balances throughput, latency, cost and reliability. We treat GPU pools as horizontally scalable, with autoscaling policies tuned per workload class (low-latency interactive vs high-throughput batch).

Key SLOs and targets:
- p95 generation latency (interactive): 250ms for baseline small-model routes, 800ms for long-context heavy models.
- Request success rate: 99.9% (error budget 0.1%) per month per region.
- Average GPU utilization target: 55-70% (buffer for spikes).
- Warm pool target: keep 10-20% of capacity warmed for low-latency tiers.

Sizing methodology (step-by-step):
1. Collect historical request distribution by model, sequence length, and time-of-day (7d/30d windows).
2. Convert to tokens/sec demand using median tokens-per-request per route.
3. Benchmark per-GPU throughput for representative model variants and batch sizes using our bench-suite (repo: infra/benchmarks/gpu-throughput).
4. Compute baseline GPU count = ceil(demand / per-GPU-throughput * safety_factor). Use safety_factor=1.35 for interactive, 1.15 for batch.
5. Allocate warm pool = ceil(baseline * warm_pool_pct).
6. Validate with chaos test: run traffic replay at 120% baseline for 1h in staging.

Cost modeling:
- Include GPU hourly price, expected utilization, average cloud egress, and amortized infra overhead. Use spreadsheet template: infra/templates/gpu-cost-model.xlsx.
- Capture reserved capacity (Dedicated) commitments versus on-demand delta.

Scaling policies and thresholds:
- Reactive autoscaler: scale_up when queue length > 5s of work or GPU avg_util > 80% for 2 consecutive 30s windows.
- Scale_down: hold_minimum 10m; scale_down when avg_util < 35% for 5m and queue empty.
- Emergency headroom policy: maintain at least 2 spare GPUs per AZ for critical-production pools.

2) Cloud accounts and networking
Account structure:
- Per-region infra accounts for core infra (cluster control plane, monitoring).
- Per-environment accounts: infra-prod, infra-staging, infra-dev.
- Customer-dedicated accounts live in their own org/project and are referenced but not managed by Redwood's core account.

VPC and subnet design:
- Use segmented VPCs per environment.
- Subnet types: private (worker nodes), utility (bastion / NAT), services (control-plane).
- Allocate /20 per region for infra-prod; reserve /24 blocks for each AZ for node pools.

Networking rules and security groups:
- Allow only required inter-subnet traffic: control-plane -> workers (gRPC/TCP 7000-7010), metrics (Prometheus 9090), SSH from bastion only (22).
- Egress: restrict public egress to approved egress-proxy endpoints via NAT.
- Peering: peer infra-prod VPC with observability and logging VPCs. Use VPC peering or PrivateLink based on cloud.

IP management and NAT:
- Use stable private IPs for GPU nodes when possible to preserve cache locality.
- NAT gateways for controlled public egress.

IAM and secrets:
- Principle of least privilege for infra service accounts.
- Use centralized KMS for GPU fleet keys (encrypt disk and KV cache).
- Access to private deployments requires scoped IAM groups and Ip allowlists.

3) Terraform / IaC modules and conventions
Principles:
- Keep modules small and single-responsibility (networking, compute, autoscaler, iam).
- Module repo: infra/modules. Publish semver tags.
- Use remote state (backend) with locking (state locking with S3+DynamoDB or Cloud Storage with locking).

Naming and variable conventions:
- Resource names: rdx-${service}-${env}-${region}-${suffix}
- Variables: "env", "region", "owner_team", "billing_code".
- Outputs: "cluster_name", "node_pool_ids", "autoscaler_id".

Module release and upgrade process:
1. Create branch infra/modules/<module>/upgrade-x.y.z.
2. Update module, add migration notes in CHANGELOG.md.
3. Run unit tests (terragrunt/terraform validate), and plan against a sandbox workspace.
4. Open PR, reviewers: infra-owners + security.
5. After merge, bump tag and run downstream plan/apply in staging pipelines.

Example compute module usage (HCL snippet):

module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo/infra/modules//compute/gpu?ref=v1.4.0"
  env = "prod"
  region = "us-west-2"
  node_count = 12
  gpu_type = "A100-80GB"
  owner_team = "serving-runtime"
}

Terraform plan gating and approvals:
- Plan automations must be allowed only for non-destructive changes. Any plan that changes >10% of nodes or modifies network/cidr requires manual approval from infra-owners.

4) CI/CD and build patterns for infra changes
Pipeline stages (recommended):
1. Validate: terraform fmt / validate, module unit tests.
2. Plan: run terraform plan with changed files; upload plan artifact.
3. Review: auto-post plan to PR; require at least one infra owner approval.
4. Apply (staging): automatic apply in staging after merge.
5. Smoke test: traffic replay + basic perf checks.
6. Promote: apply to prod via gated pipeline (manual approval + scheduled 30m maintenance window).

Best practices:
- All infra changes must be idempotent and reversible.
- Keep plan artifacts and diffs in PRs for auditability.
- Use feature toggles for large capacity changes; ramp up with canary pools (10% -> 30% -> 100%).
- CI secrets: use vault-backed credentials with short-lived tokens for pipelines.

Example pipeline commands (CLI):
- validate: terraform -chdir=env/prod fmt -check && terraform -chdir=env/prod validate
- plan: terraform -chdir=env/prod plan -out=plan.tfplan
- apply: terraform -chdir=env/prod apply "plan.tfplan"

5) Runbooks (high priority incidents)
A. Incident: cluster autoscaler failing to scale up (symptoms: queue growth, p95 latency spikes)
1. Check autoscaler logs: kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/cluster-autoscaler | tail -n 200
2. Check node group limits: aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups --region $REGION --query "AutoScalingGroups[?AutoScalingGroupName=='rdx-*']"
3. Ensure cloud quotas not exhausted (GPUs per region). If quota exhausted, escalate to cloud-ops and open quota request ticket - tag: quota-emergency.
4. If ASG healthy but no instances launching, check launch template/instance profile IAM role and subnet availability.
5. Temporary mitigation: scale up warm pool manually (terraform apply -var 'node_count=+3') and route canary traffic to warm pool.
6. Postmortem: capture root cause, mitigation, ETA to fully recover; update runbook.

B. Incident: GPU node OOM / kernel crash (symptoms: OOM events, pods evicted, node reboot)
1. Drain node: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
2. Collect logs: journalctl -u docker -o short-iso --since "1 hour ago" > /tmp/node-logs.txt; nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used --format=csv -l 1 > /tmp/gpu-mem-sample.csv
3. Recreate node pool if repeated: cordon the pool and create replacement nodes via module with incremented node_count.
4. If hardware fault suspected, tag node with 'hw-fault' and open ticket with cloud provider with attached diagnostics.

C. Incident: networking partition between control-plane and workers
1. Verify security group rules and routing tables.
2. Check VPC route tables and NAT gateway status.
3. If route table changed in terraform: revert via pipeline to last successful plan.
4. If partition persists, failover traffic to alternate AZ region (follow failover checklist in infra/runbooks/failover-checklist).

Post-incident steps (always):
- Declare incident severity and notify owners.
- Create postmortem within 72 hours and link to this playbook.
- Add regression tests and monitor alert tuning to prevent recurrence.

6) Operational telemetry, dashboards and ownership
Critical metrics to monitor:
- Queue length and token backlog per model route.
- GPU utilization (avg, p50/p95), temperature and memory usage.
- Node boot time and provisioning failures.
- Autoscaler actions (scale_up/scale_down events).
- P95 latency and error rate per route/model.
- Cost per token and per-hour GPU spend.

Dashboards and alerts:
- Dashboards live in grafana/infra/gpu-fleet-overview.
- Alerts: p95 latency > SLO for 10m, queue_length > threshold, GPU_util > 85% for 5m, node_boot_failures > 3 in 15m.

Ownership and runbook contacts:
- Fleet ownership: infra-gpu-team@redwood.com (primary), serving-runtime@redwood.com (secondary).
- Oncall rotation: infra-oncall (2-week cadence).
- Pager escalation: page infra-owner -> if not acknowledged in 15m escalate to infra-eng lead.

Appendix: templates and useful commands
- Cost model: infra/templates/gpu-cost-model.xlsx
- Plan gating checklist: infra/checklists/plan-gating.md
- Terraform backend examples: infra/modules/backends/README.md

Quick CLI snippets:
- Check queued requests: rdxctl metrics queue --model rdx-llama-13b --window 5m
- Warmup a node pool: terraform -chdir=env/prod apply -var 'node_count=3' -target=module.gpu_node_pool

Governance and change control:
- Any change that impacts more than 5% of production capacity requires a Change Advisory Review (CAR) and a scheduled maintenance window.
- Security-sensitive changes (IAM, KMS, network ACLs) must be reviewed by security team and marked as restricted if customer-impacting.
